key_insight: During nanoscratch of 316H stainless steel, the martensitic transformation follows a pressure- and shear-controlled sequence of γ-austenite → ε-martensite → α′-martensite, with hydrostatic constraint favoring ε and sliding shear promoting α′.
engineering_relevance: This reveals how local contact mechanics govern tribolayer formation and galling behavior, helping guide alloy and surface design for improved wear resistance.
method: In-situ synchrotron X-ray nanodiffractometry during nanoscratch testing
Spatial mapping of evolving strain and martensite phase distribution beneath a single sliding asperity
Finite element modeling to interpret stress states and pathway selection
evidence_signal: The abstract reports spatially resolved in-situ measurements combined with FEM that distinguish competing martensitic pathways and link phase selection to local hydrostatic pressure and shear strain.
watch_item: The conclusions are based on a single-asperity nanoscratch experiment, so translation to real multi-asperity service contacts and larger-scale tribolayers may require additional validation.
paper_title: Spatially resolved in-situ characterisation of competing martensitic transformation pathways during nanoscratch in 316H Stainless Steel
